name: LangChain
description: Agent engineering framework with tool-calling agent loop and large integrations ecosystem
scored_configuration: The langchain v1 create_agent API with default arguments (no middleware, no checkpointer or store, tracing off), plus the bundled opt-in middleware and MCP adapter at their constructor defaults.
headline: LangChain gives you a tool-calling agent loop and leaves almost every safety control to you. As shipped, create_agent runs every tool call with no approval, no untrusted-input containment, no authorization layer and a 9,999-step limit, so a prompt-injected agent can do anything its tools allow. Good controls exist as opt-in middleware (per-call human approval showing exact arguments, call limits, PII redaction, a Docker shell policy), but the bundled shell tool defaults to unisolated host execution.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: LangChain has no identity or authorization layer of its own. An agent built with create_agent runs every tool with whatever credentials the developer's code and the host process hold, and nothing checks a tool call against a policy or the requesting user. The one narrowing found is accidental-looking: the opt-in shell tool starts with an empty environment when no env is passed, although its docstring says it inherits the parent environment. If an agent is hijacked, the attacker gets the full authority of the process.

S.finding: Tools run with the ambient authority of the developer's process; the framework offers no scoped-identity or credential-narrowing primitive.
S.gap: No per-tool or per-request credential scoping or authorization gate in code.

evidence.note: one is a PermissionError catch in file_search, one is the HITL edit-notice text; no authorization layer exists

C.finding: Every tool, including MCP and middleware tools, constructs or receives its own clients; no shared authorization check sits on the tool path.
C.gap: No authorization layer that every tool path traverses.

evidence.note: one is a PermissionError catch in file_search, one is the HITL edit-notice text; no authorization layer exists

D.finding: The default create_agent applies no privilege restriction; the agent holds whatever the launching user and the passed tools hold.
D.gap: No narrower default identity; least privilege is entirely developer work.

B.finding: Nothing the framework does bounds a hijacked agent's authority; with the bundled shell tool on its default host policy, the agent reaches every file and credential store the OS user can (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, kubeconfig).
B.gap: Framework-enforced scoping that keeps a hijacked agent below the user's full cross-service authority.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: By default create_agent executes every tool call the model emits with no human approval. LangChain ships a good opt-in HumanInTheLoopMiddleware that pauses on listed tools, shows the exact tool name and arguments, and supports approve, edit, reject and respond, with edits applied exactly at execution. But it only gates tools named in its map; any tool not listed, including MCP tools added later, is auto-approved, and nothing offers undo or rollback for actions already taken.

cap.reason: Opt-in mechanism: off in the scored default configuration.

S.finding: Per-call interrupt showing the exact tool name and arguments, with per-tool decision sets and an optional when predicate; reviewer edits are substituted at execution time.
S.gap: No argument-level deny rules; the when predicate can only escalate or auto-approve.

C.finding: Only tools listed in interrupt_on are gated; any unlisted tool, including MCP tools discovered later, is auto-approved.
C.gap: Reject or gate unknown tools by default so every path traverses the gate.

D.finding: The middleware must be added explicitly; create_agent's middleware default is empty.
D.gap: Approval on by default.

B.finding: Same as default: no undo or rollback for actions an approver wrongly allows.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Every LangChain tool with a Pydantic schema has its arguments type-checked before it runs, which stops malformed calls but is not an allowlist. Tools defined with a raw JSON schema, which is how MCP tools are adapted, skip validation entirely. The bundled file-search tool does resolved, symlink-aware path containment, but the bundled shell tool accepts any command string. No tools are enabled unless the developer passes them, but the framework has no read/write tiering of its own.

S.finding: Pydantic schema validation on tool input; FileSearchMiddleware adds resolved-path containment, but the shell tool is raw passthrough.
S.gap: Allowlist validation (paths, hosts, commands) as a framework primitive, not only in one bundled tool.

C.finding: Schema validation applies to every BaseModel-typed tool, but dict (JSON-schema) tools such as MCP tools return their input unvalidated.
C.gap: A shared validation layer that also covers dict-schema and MCP tools.

D.finding: No tools are enabled by default; whatever the developer passes is live with no read/write distinction, and middleware can add tools such as the shell.
D.gap: A read-only default tool tier with write/exec requiring explicit elevation.

B.finding: The framework itself bounds little: the shell tool has a 30-second per-command timeout and output caps but can run any command anywhere the user can.
B.gap: Workspace scoping enforced for general-purpose tools.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: LangChain's code-execution surface is the opt-in ShellToolMiddleware, and when a developer enables it without choosing a policy it runs a persistent bash shell directly on the host, with no filesystem or network isolation. A Docker execution policy is available that runs commands in a separate container with networking off and the container removed afterwards, and it fails rather than falling back to the host when Docker is missing. That container is stock, though: root inside, default capabilities, no resource limits by default, and the developer's workspace mounted read-write when one is configured. Local MCP servers launched over stdio always run on the host.

cap.reason: Opt-in mechanism: off in the scored default configuration.

S.finding: A stock docker run container: no --user by default, no capability drop, no seccomp/no-new-privileges flags.
S.gap: Hardened container defaults: non-root user, dropped capabilities, no-new-privileges.

C.finding: Covers the shell tool only; MCP stdio servers and other tools still run on the host process.
C.gap: Sandbox every model-reachable execution path, including MCP stdio servers.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Tool results, including web, file and MCP content, are appended to the conversation as tool messages and fed straight back to the model, and nothing in the framework tracks taint, quarantines untrusted text, or disables egress or state-changing tools once untrusted content has been read. MCP tool descriptions are passed to the model verbatim. Because LangChain's own documentation combines untrusted inputs, private data and outbound tools in ordinary use, a successful prompt injection can both leak data and take irreversible actions without a human.

cap.reason: Worst case (B L0): a hijacked agent can leak data and take irreversible actions unattended.

S.finding: No structural limit on a hijacked agent: no taint tracking, no Rule-of-Two enforcement, no quarantined-LLM pattern.
S.gap: Force egress and state-changing tools through approval once untrusted content enters a session.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: LangChain loads no instruction files or .env files from the working directory, and by default create_agent keeps state only in memory for a single run. Persistence is opt-in through a LangGraph checkpointer (per conversation thread) or store, and when enabled the saved conversation, including untrusted tool output, is reloaded verbatim with no validation, expiry or review. The opt-in summarization middleware re-injects a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user-role message, so injected text can be laundered into something that looks like the user's own instructions.

S.finding: Persisted state is reloaded unvalidated; summaries of untrusted content come back as a HumanMessage, losing provenance.
S.gap: Present persisted and summarized content as data with provenance, or gate memory writes.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: LangChain's runtime extension path is MCP: the beta MCPAdapter connects to servers the developer names and exposes every tool they advertise. String targets are refused unless they are http(s) URLs, so a string cannot silently launch a local script. But there is no version pinning, hash check, or re-approval when a server's tools or descriptions change between runs, and stdio servers run as local processes under the same user.

S.finding: Developer-chosen MCP targets, re-listed on each connection with no pinning or integrity check.
S.gap: Pin server versions or verify integrity of what is launched.

C.finding: No extension type is verified.

D.finding: Nothing is enabled by default; a developer must name each target in code, and bare strings that would launch a subprocess are refused.

B.finding: Remote MCP servers run off-host; local stdio servers run as separate processes, and the upstream MCP SDK passes a reduced default environment (third-party behaviour, not in this repo).

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: Model API keys are held as Pydantic SecretStr values and are swapped for secret references when LangChain objects are serialized, and the framework ships no telemetry or crash reporting. The opt-in shell tool starts with an empty environment unless the developer passes one, so it does not inherit API keys through its environment. Nothing redacts secrets or personal data from what is sent to the model by default; PII and output redaction are opt-in, and LangSmith tracing, when switched on, uploads full inputs and outputs.

S.finding: Type-level masking (SecretStr) and secret stripping on serialization.
S.gap: Redaction before model-bound messages and traces on all major paths.

C.finding: Serialized objects and the shell subprocess environment are protected; model-bound messages and traces are not by default.
C.gap: Cover model-bound messages and tracing payloads.

D.finding: No telemetry SDKs; tracing is opt-in via environment; redaction middleware is opt-in.
D.gap: Always-on redaction for traces and logs.

B.finding: Long-lived provider API keys sit in the process; a same-user host shell can still read them from the parent's /proc environ or credential files.
B.gap: Short-lived or scoped credentials.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: By default the only record of what an agent did is the in-memory message list returned to the caller, which holds each tool call's name, arguments and result but no timestamps, and is lost if the process crashes unless a checkpointer is configured. LangChain integrates with LangSmith tracing, which records structured, nested runs for every model and tool call and ships them off the machine, but it is opt-in via environment variables and does not record who requested or approved an action.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: create_agent sets LangGraph's recursion limit to 9,999 steps, which is an iteration cap in name only, and there is no default wall-clock, token or cost limit. Opt-in middleware can cap model calls and tool calls per run or per thread, but their limits default to none. A sub-agent built with create_agent gets its own fresh 9,999-step limit. The shell tool does enforce a 30-second per-command timeout and kills the whole process group when it fires.

S.finding: Iteration cap only (9,999 steps); no default wall-clock or cost cap; call-limit middleware is opt-in.
S.gap: Add a default wall-clock or token/cost cap enforced in code.

evidence.note: no time or cost budget in the agent factory

C.finding: The cap applies to the top-level loop; each sub-agent agent compiled by create_agent carries its own 9,999 limit.
C.gap: Make sub-agents count against the parent's budget.

D.finding: The default limit is very large.
D.gap: Sensible default limits.

B.finding: A runaway can make thousands of model and tool calls before the cap trips.
B.gap: Tight per-run time and cost ceilings.

critical_findings.summary: No identity scoping or authorization layer: a hijacked agent acts with the full ambient authority of the developer's process, and the bundled shell tool defaults to unisolated host execution.
The bundled shell tool defaults to HostExecutionPolicy: model-generated commands run as the host user with no filesystem or network isolation.
No untrusted-input containment: injected tool or MCP content can drive both data exfiltration and irreversible tool actions with no human in the loop by default.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: Tool and MCP results re-enter the model as ToolMessages (libs/langchain_v1/langchain/agents/factory.py:1021)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: Ambient developer credentials and host files reachable by tools; shell defaults to host (libs/langchain_v1/langchain/agents/middleware/shell_tool.py:594)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: Any registered tool runs without approval by default (libs/langchain_v1/langchain/agents/factory.py:897)

fixes.summary: Make ShellToolMiddleware default to DockerExecutionPolicy (or refuse to start without an explicit policy) instead of HostExecutionPolicy.
Have HumanInTheLoopMiddleware gate unlisted tools by default (deny or interrupt unknown tools) rather than auto-approving them.
Lower the default recursion limit and add a default wall-clock/token budget shared with sub-agents.
Return summaries as a distinct, provenance-tagged message type rather than a HumanMessage.
Validate dict/JSON-schema (including MCP) tool inputs against their schema before execution.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.
No release tag points at the pinned commit; libs/langchain_v1/pyproject.toml declares langchain 1.4.3.

Scope is the monorepo at the pinned commit with the langchain v1 create_agent path as the primary deployment; langchain-classic (legacy) and partner integrations were sampled, not exhaustively reviewed.

The agent loop's ToolNode, checkpointer namespacing, interrupt/resume and LangSmith upload behaviour live in the out-of-repo langgraph and langsmith libraries; ratings relying on them are marked inferred.
MCP stdio environment handling comes from the third-party fastmcp/mcp SDK and was not verified in this repository.
No reviewer-directed prompt injection was found; AGENTS.md contains development-tool instructions for coding agents (Corridor security analysis), treated as data.
